title: Protecting breastfeeding in all settings
blurb: Know the law on breastfeeding in public, work within the WHO Code, and team up with agencies and communities to protect breastfeeding.
question: Kemi, a community midwife, is offered free branded notepads and a sponsored study day by a formula company. The same week, a woman tells her a café asked her to stop breastfeeding her 10-week-old. How should Kemi respond to each?

teach.body: Formally, midwives work with other professionals, agencies and communities to promote, support and protect breastfeeding, including protection for women to breastfeed in all settings (SPM 2.10). In plain English: helping a woman to latch is support; telling her the benefits is promotion; protection means defending her right to feed anywhere and keeping commercial pressure out of infant feeding decisions.

teach.caption: NG194 1.5.5: tell women and partners they have the right to breastfeed in any public space.

teach.h: How the Equality Act protects her
teach.body: Section 17: in the 26 weeks from the day she gives birth, treating a woman unfavourably because she is breastfeeding is pregnancy and maternity discrimination in services, premises, education and associations. After 26 weeks, section 13(6)(a) applies: less favourable treatment of a woman because she is breastfeeding is sex discrimination. So the protection continues as her baby grows.

teach.caption: Aim (Article 1): safe, adequate infant nutrition by protecting breastfeeding and ensuring proper use of substitutes when needed.

head: Prohibited
What it looks like

A free study day with lunch
teach.caption: The Code applies to health workers whatever a country's legal framework. It does not ban sales or factual information about formula.

teach.body: Kemi declines the notepads and the sponsored study day: the Code bars gifts and sponsorship, and the NMC Code asks her to refuse all but the most trivial gifts that could be seen as seeking preferential treatment (21.1). To the mother, she explains that the café acted unlawfully: her baby is under 26 weeks, so refusing service because she is breastfeeding is pregnancy and maternity discrimination. Kemi shares the local breastfeeding-welcome scheme with community partners.
teach.cite: WHO Code; NMC Code 21.1; Equality Act 2010 s17

teach.text: Protecting breastfeeding does NOT mean refusing help to parents who formula feed. The Code does not stop factual, non-commercial information on safe formula feeding; NICE asks for independent, evidence-based formula advice, and Baby Friendly says formula-feeding families must not be denied information or care.

items: SPM 2.10: promote, support and protect breastfeeding, including in all settings.
Equality Act: s17 for 26 weeks after birth, then s13(6)(a) sex discrimination.
Scotland: offence to stop a child under 2 being fed milk in a public place.
WHO Code 1981: no promotion, samples, gifts or sponsorship; formula bought at full price.
Support formula-feeding parents with factual, non-commercial information.

summary: You can now explain the legal right to breastfeed in public across Great Britain, apply the WHO Code to everyday encounters with industry, and work with agencies and communities to protect breastfeeding while still supporting families who formula feed.

A.q: In England, a café owner asks Lucy to leave because she is breastfeeding her 10-week-old baby. Under the Equality Act 2010, what is this?
options: Pregnancy and maternity discrimination under s17
Lawful, if other customers have complained
Lawful, if the café offers a private room
Unlawful in Scotland but lawful in England
A.why: Section 17(3)-(4): within 26 weeks of giving birth, treating a woman unfavourably because she is breastfeeding is pregnancy and maternity discrimination in services.

whyNot.1: Complaints from others do not make discrimination lawful.
whyNot.2: Offering a private room does not justify asking her to leave.
whyNot.3: The Equality Act protects her in England, Wales and Scotland.

A.q: The Breastfeeding etc. (Scotland) Act 2005 makes it an offence to stop someone feeding milk to a child in a public place. Up to what age of child does it apply?
options: Under 6 months
Under 1 year
Under 2 years
Under 26 weeks
A.why: Section 1 of the 2005 Act defines a child as a person who has not yet reached 2 years of age.

whyNot.0: Six months is not the Scottish Act's limit.
whyNot.1: One year is shorter than the 2-year limit.
whyNot.3: 26 weeks is the Equality Act s17 period, not the Scottish Act.

A.q: In which year did the World Health Assembly adopt the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes?
A.why: The Code was adopted by the World Health Assembly on 21 May 1981.

whyNot.1: 1989 is not the year the Code was adopted; that was 1981.
whyNot.2: 1991 is a decade after the Code was adopted in 1981.
whyNot.3: 2010 is the year of the Equality Act.

B.q: A formula company representative leaves branded notepads and pens at the community midwives' office. What should the midwives do?
options: Keep items that do not show a formula brand
Use them for staff but keep them from parents
Decline them, as the Code bars gifts to staff
Keep them once they are added to a gifts register
B.why: The WHO Code bars companies from giving free samples, gifts or promotional materials to health workers or families. NMC Code 21.1: refuse all but the most trivial gifts.

whyNot.0: Company gifts are prohibited whether or not branded.
whyNot.1: The prohibition covers gifts to health workers as well as to families.
whyNot.3: Registering a gift does not make a Code-breaching gift acceptable.

B.q: In a Baby Friendly accredited unit, Holly has decided to formula feed and asks how to make up feeds safely. What should the midwife do?
options: Explain that formula is not discussed in Baby Friendly units
Give factual, non-commercial guidance on making up feeds
Give her a leaflet from a formula brand's starter pack
Refer her to a formula company's customer helpline
B.why: The Code does not prohibit factual information about bottle feeding, and Baby Friendly says families who formula feed must not be denied information or care. NICE asks for independent, non-commercial formula advice.

whyNot.0: Withholding information is not what the Code or Baby Friendly require.
whyNot.2: Branded material is commercial promotion within the Code's scope.
whyNot.3: Company helplines are commercial sources, not independent advice.

B.q: Asha is asked to leave a restaurant in Wales because she is breastfeeding her 9-month-old. Which part of the Equality Act protects her?
options: Section 17, as protection lasts 12 months
None, as protection ends at 26 weeks
Section 20, as a reasonable adjustment
Section 13, as sex discrimination
B.why: After the 26-week s17 period, s13(6)(a) applies: less favourable treatment of a woman because she is breastfeeding is sex discrimination.

whyNot.0: Section 17 protection lasts 26 weeks from birth, not 12 months.
whyNot.1: Protection continues through s13(6)(a) after 26 weeks.
whyNot.2: Section 20 concerns adjustments for disabled people.

C.q: A formula manufacturer offers the maternity unit a free year's supply of ready-to-feed formula. What is the correct response under the Code and Baby Friendly standards?
options: Accept it if every brand donates an equal amount
Accept it for the neonatal unit where need is greatest
Accept it and record it as a charitable donation
Decline it and buy formula at full market price
C.why: Services must buy formula at full market price through NHS Supply Chain or retail, and should not accept free or discounted supplies, so procurement stays free of commercial influence.

whyNot.0: Equal donations are still free supplies that create commercial influence.
whyNot.1: Neonatal units are bound by the same procurement principles.
whyNot.2: Calling it a donation does not change its promotional effect.

C.q: Nadia plans to return to work when her baby is 6 months old and wants to keep breastfeeding. Which advice best follows NICE NG247?
options: Switch to formula in the month before returning
Stop breastfeeding 2 weeks before returning
Tell her employer early and plan expressing
Express at home, as workplaces cannot be asked
C.why: NG247: reassure people they do not need to stop breastfeeding when they return to work, encourage them to tell their employer in good time, and discuss support such as a private, hygienic space to express and storage.

whyNot.0: NICE reassures women they do not need to stop.
whyNot.1: Stopping is unnecessary; planning support is the advice.
whyNot.3: Employers can provide space, storage and breaks, and should be asked.

C.q: Chantelle, 18, lives on a low income and has just started breastfeeding. Which plan best protects her breastfeeding?
options: A leaflet and the national breastfeeding helpline
Formula vouchers in case breastfeeding fails
A telephone review on day 10 with her midwife
Face-to-face support, continuity and peer support
C.why: NG194 1.5.9-1.5.11: give face-to-face support with continuity of carer and peer support; younger and low-income women may need more support, and continuity is particularly important for them.

whyNot.0: Written information supplements but does not replace face-to-face support.
whyNot.1: Offering formula undermines her chosen feeding method.
whyNot.2: A single phone review is too little, too late.

reteach.title: A shield with three layers
reteach.question: What protects a breastfeeding woman: in the café, in the clinic, and in her community?

blocks.body: Layer one is the law: the Equality Act (s17 for 26 weeks, then s13 sex discrimination) and, in Scotland, a criminal offence to stop a child under 2 being fed. Layer two is the WHO Code: no marketing, samples, gifts or sponsorship in health services. Layer three is community: peer supporters, employers and businesses that welcome breastfeeding.

blocks.text: The s17 protection ends at 26 weeks, but the right does not: s13(6)(a) sex discrimination covers breastfeeding after that.

explain.body: Equality Act s17: 26 weeks from birth, unfavourable treatment for breastfeeding is pregnancy and maternity discrimination. After that, s13(6)(a) sex discrimination. Scotland also has a criminal offence for stopping a child under 2 from being fed milk in public or licensed premises.

test.q: For how long after the birth does Equality Act s17 protect a woman from unfavourable treatment because she is breastfeeding?
options: 26 weeks
12 months
2 years
6 weeks
test.why: Section 17(3)-(4) protects her in the period of 26 weeks beginning with the day she gives birth.

whyNot.1: 12 months is not the s17 period.
whyNot.2: 2 years is the Scottish Act's child age limit.
whyNot.3: 6 weeks is the postnatal period used elsewhere, not s17.

explain.body: Adopted in 1981 to protect breastfeeding and ensure proper use of substitutes. Companies may not promote in health services or to the public, give samples or gifts, sponsor meetings, or use idealising labels. It applies to health workers whatever national law says.

test.q: Which products does the WHO Code cover?
options: Breastmilk substitutes up to 36 months, bottles and teats
First infant formula for babies under 6 months
Breast pumps and nipple creams sold in pharmacies
Weaning foods for children over 3 years old
test.why: The Code covers breastmilk substitutes marketed for use up to 36 months, including follow-on and growing-up milks, plus feeding bottles and teats.

whyNot.1: Coverage extends beyond first formula to products up to 36 months, plus bottles and teats.
whyNot.2: Breast pumps and creams are not the Code's focus.
whyNot.3: The Code's scope ends at 36 months.

explain.body: Baby Friendly services adhere to the Code: no advertising of formula, bottles, teats or food for babies under 6 months; formula bought at full market price; teaching free from company involvement. Families who formula feed still get full, factual information and care.

test.q: How should a Baby Friendly maternity unit obtain the infant formula it needs for babies who require it?
options: Free supplies from manufacturers
Discounted bulk deals with one brand
Purchase at full market price
Donations collected from families
test.why: Services must purchase infant formula at full market price through NHS Supply Chain or retail outlets, without free or discounted supplies.

whyNot.1: Negotiated discounts with companies are not permitted.
whyNot.3: Unregulated donated formula is not an appropriate supply route.

explain.body: Give face-to-face support with continuity and peer support (NG194 1.5.9); extra support for younger and low-income women (1.5.11); tell women about the right to feed in public (1.5.5); help women plan breastfeeding on return to work with employers (NG247).

test.q: According to NICE NG194, which women may need more support to start and continue breastfeeding?
options: Women having a second baby
Younger and low-income women
Women who had a caesarean birth
Women who breastfed before
test.why: NG194 1.5.11: younger women and those from low-income or disadvantaged backgrounds may need more support, and continuity of carer is particularly important for them.

whyNot.0: Parity is not the factor NG194 1.5.11 names.
whyNot.2: Caesarean birth is not named in NG194 1.5.11.
whyNot.3: Previous breastfeeding is not a group named in NG194 1.5.11.
